title: The King Who Longed for a Child
captions: Long ago, on the banks of the river Sarayu, stood the golden city of Ayodhya.
Its king, Dasharatha, was brave and fair. His people loved him, and the kingdom had everything it needed.
But the king carried one sorrow. He had no child, and no heir to care for Ayodhya after him.
His teacher, the sage Vasishtha, told him: "Do not lose hope. Hold a sacred fire ceremony and pray with a true heart."
The fire blazed, and from it rose a shining messenger carrying a golden bowl of blessed sweet rice.
The king shared the gift among his three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra.
In time, four princes were born. All of Ayodhya rejoiced!
story: Long ago, the kingdom of Kosala lay along the banks of the river Sarayu. Its capital was Ayodhya, a city of wide streets, tall gates and busy markets, where people lived in peace. Its ruler was King Dasharatha of the Ikshvaku family, the line of the Sun. He was a brave warrior and a fair judge, and his people trusted him completely.
Yet the king carried a quiet sorrow. He had three queens, Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra, but no children. Who would care for Ayodhya when he grew old? The thought stayed with him day and night.

The king did not keep his worry to himself. He went to his family guru, the wise sage Vasishtha, and opened his heart. Vasishtha listened and gave him hope. He advised a sacred fire ceremony, a yajna, offered with prayer and devotion. Great sages came to help, and the whole court joined in.

As the offerings went into the fire, the flames rose high and bright. From them appeared a shining being holding a golden bowl of blessed sweet rice, called payasam. The messenger gave it to the king as a gift from the gods.

Dasharatha did not keep the blessing for one queen. He shared it among all three. In time, four sons were born: Rama to Kausalya, Bharata to Kaikeyi, and the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna to Sumitra. Ayodhya celebrated with music, lamps and feasts.
lesson: King Dasharatha was sad, but he did not give up. He bowed to his guru, listened to his advice, and prayed with a true heart. Our elders teach that when we pray with shraddha, do our part and wait patiently, blessings come at the right time. And when the blessing came, the king shared it.
lesson_long: Shraddha means faith with a true heart. It is more than wishing for something. It is trusting, doing your part, and being patient.

Look at what King Dasharatha did. He was sad, but he did not give up or sit alone with his worry. He went to his guru, listened carefully, and followed the advice. He prayed with his whole heart and then waited. Our elders teach that this is how shraddha works: we pray, we act, and we trust that good things come at the right time.
There is a second lesson hidden in the story. When the blessing came, the king shared it with all three queens. In our tradition, a blessing grows when it is shared.
tradition: The fire ceremony in this story is called the Putrakameshti yajna, a prayer for children. Fire, or Agni, has a special place in Hindu worship. Agni is seen as the messenger who carries our offerings and prayers to the gods. That is why a lamp or a sacred fire is still lit at weddings, housewarmings and festivals today.

The sweet rice the king shared is like prasadam, food that is first offered to God and then comes back to us as a blessing. When we receive prasadam at a temple, we accept it with respect and share it with family and friends, just as Dasharatha did.
words: the capital city of King Dasharatha, on the river Sarayu
a teacher who guides us, in learning and in life
a sacred fire ceremony with prayers and offerings
the sacred fire, and the deity of fire
food offered to God and shared as a blessing
question: Who is a guru in your life, like a parent, a grandparent or a teacher? What good advice have they given you?
questions: Who is a guru in your life, like a parent, a grandparent or a teacher? What good advice have they given you?
Have you ever waited a long time for something you hoped for? How did you stay patient?
Why do you think the king shared the sweet rice with all three queens instead of just one?
